## "And though she be but little, she is fierce"

# Alternative Fairy Tales: Hänsel and Gretel

I have decided to start a running series of short stories with the theme Alternative Fairy Tales.This will be my first addition to the series, the story of Hänsel and Gretel.If you are not familiar with the story, the following link will take you to the Brothers Grimm’s version of the tale: 

Constructive criticism is appreciated!

Sweet Tooth [...] This just made the child cry harder, her sobs turning her damp face as red as the strawberry chews that were scattered by her feet.

“Not Hänsel, please not Hänsel,” she continued in a shaky voice.

This last plea made the Witch pause for a minute, a flicker of realisation flashing across her face. Could it be? She set down the cooking pot once more and carefully looked the girl up and down, chewing on her lips with her yellowing teeth. Despite having hoarded these children, she had not once learnt their names. It just didn’t occur to her. She didn’t often play with her food like this, let alone make pleasantries with it.

“Hänsel, you say? A pitiful name to suit such a weed of a boy,” she eventually replied. “And what would yours be?” [...] Gretel’s instant reflex was to run, and before she knew it her legs were carrying her through the house and to the front door. Just as she got her hands on the handle, a trickle of guilt ran through her, unable to get the image of poor Hänsel, alone in the kitchen, out of her head. In the midst of her fleeting pause, Gretel was seized from behind and carried back to the kitchen.

“You may be a quick little worm but you’re not as strong as me!” cried the Witch, dumping Gretel in the brass pot, her body crumpled on top of her brother’s. The lid was then forced over them, and Bertel hauled the heavy load into the oven, slamming the door.

There’s the indelible bond of these siblings too, a boy and girl, not unlike the characters in The Snow Queen.

Hansel and Gretel by Cynthia Rylant, pictures by Jen Corace (2008).

This version has a classic feel and is well-suited for younger readers. Despite the disturbing nature of the familiar tale, there’s a sense that all will be well, that children are meant to be loved and cherished and looked after and, ultimately, they will be. Not to worry, Hansel and Gretel will prevail by way of love and ingenuity and their own strength.

running-home(click image(s) to enlarge)

From the beginning: [...] This is a story with lessons for children, and not cloying ones. Real lessons. Hard lessons. Lessons of their own wisdom and resilience despite dangers.

Images via JenCorace.com.

Hansel & Gretel by Neil Gaiman and Lorenzo Mattotti (2014).

This newer version (someday to be a film)) is a darker take. So so so very dark and definitely suited for slightly older readers.

The full-spread illustrations are in solely black and white. Inky, scary, hard to decipher. It was, in fact, Mattotti’s artwork from an exhibit at The Metropolitan Operathat inspired Gaiman’s story.

Hansel & Gretel and the Enchanted Castle (1995) by Terraglyph Interactive Studios is an adventure and hidden object game. The player controls Hansel, tasked with finding Prin, a forest imp, who holds the key to saving Gretel from the witch.
 Gretel and Hansel (2009) by Mako Pudding is a browser adventure game. Popular on Newgrounds for its gruesome reimagining of the story, it features hand-painted watercolor backgrounds and characters animated by Flash.
 Fearful Tales: Hansel and Gretel Collector's Edition (2013) by Eipix Entertainment is a HOPA (hidden object puzzle adventure) game. The player, as Hansel and Gretel's mother, searches the witch's lair for clues. [...] Hansel and Gretel: An Opera Fantasy, a 1954 stop-motion animated theatrical feature film directed by John Paul and released by RKO Radio Pictures.
 Bewitched Bunny, a 1954 Bugs Bunny cartoon directed by Chuck Jones, is a parody of Hansel and Gretel, and the debut of the Witch Hazel "Witch Hazel (Looney Tunes)") character.
 The Bewitched episode "Hansel and Gretel in Samanthaland" has Tabitha Stephens magically switching places with Hansel and Gretel, and her mother, Samantha, entering the fairy tale to rescue her from the child-eating witch. The episode features Bobo Lewis as the stepmother, Billie Hayes as the witch, and Richard X. Slattery as a policeman.

"Hansel and Gretel" (/ˈhænsəl, ˈhɛn- ... ˈɡrɛtəl/; German: Hänsel und Gretel ( "Help:IPA/Standard German")) is a German fairy tale collected by the Brothers Grimm and published in 1812 as part of Grimms' Fairy Tales (KHM 15).

results.title: Grimm Brothers’ Hansel and Gretel
results.content: The 1857 Grimms’ variant of this tale combines several significant motifs including the wicked stepmother (a change from the evil mother figure in the Grimms’ 1812 version of the same tale), the abandonment of children, the trail of crumbs (or peas) consumed by birds, the edible house (similar to the candy houses in the Land of Cockaigne, the mythical medieval land of plenty), and the cannibalistic witch (or ogre) who is tricked into climbing into their own oven.

results.content:
God is gracious.

### Variations

Anselm, Hansen, Mansel

The name "Hansel" is of Germanic origin and is traditionally considered a diminutive form of the name "Hans," which itself is a derivative of "Johannes," the Latin form of "John." The name "Hansel" can be interpreted to mean "little Hans" or "son of Hans," with "Hans" meaning "God is gracious." As a diminutive, "Hansel" carries connotations of affection and endearment, often used to denote a younger or smaller version of someone named Hans. [...] Historically, the name "Hansel" has been relatively uncommon as a standalone name, with the name "Hans" being more widely used in German-speaking countries. However, the use of "Hansel" has been influenced by its association with the fairy tale, leading to occasional use in various cultures, particularly in families with a fondness for fairy tales or German heritage. It is also worth noting that the name has seen variations and adaptations in different languages and regions, which may alter its prevalence and usage. [...] In modern times, the name "Hansel" is less frequently encountered as a first name, although it remains recognizable due to its literary and cultural ties. The name has found a place in popular culture, notably through various adaptations of "Hansel and Gretel," where characters named Hansel continue to embody the traits of bravery and cleverness. In addition, the character of Hansel has been portrayed in numerous films, stage productions, and animated adaptations, contributing to its recognition and association with childhood and fantasy.
